title: The sacred spring
text: Hot water rises here at 46 °C, over a million litres a day. Before the Romans it was a shrine of the Brythonic goddess Sulis; the Romans linked her with Minerva and began a temple complex in the AD 60s. 130 curse tablets were later found in the spring.

title: Temple of Sulis Minerva
text: The temple stood on a podium over two metres high; its pediment, 7.9 m wide, carried a Gorgon-type head about 15 m up. A gilt bronze head of Minerva was found nearby in 1727.

title: Aquae Sulis
text: The baths grew over 300 years, and in the 2nd century were enclosed in a barrel-vaulted building with hot, warm and cold rooms. The walls, probably 3rd century, enclosed about 9.3 hectares around the religious centre, where the Fosse Way crossed the Avon.
check: The wall line here follows the medieval walls, which kept the Roman line; it is approximate.

title: The lost baths
text: After Rome the baths fell into disrepair and were lost to silting and flooding. In the 12th century John of Tours built a curative bath over the King's Spring, and in the 16th century the city built the Queen's Bath.

title: The Pump Room
text: Begun by Thomas Baldwin in 1789 and completed by John Palmer in 1799, where fashionable visitors came to drink the waters.

title: The Royal Crescent
text: John Wood the Younger's crescent of 30 houses behind one 150 m front of 114 Ionic columns: the first crescent of terraced houses, looking over parkland. Buyers bought a length of facade and built their own houses behind it.

title: Georgian Bath in the model
text: The Georgian view keeps today's buildings within the Georgian city and leaves out the rest: a rough cut, since many later buildings stand inside it and some Georgian ones outside.
